# A mouse in the elevated plus maze {#sec-movement-mouse}

In this case study, we'll use [`movement`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/) to analyse a mouse navigating an elevated plus maze (EPM)—a widely used behavioural assay for measuring anxiety in rodents.
Our goal is to quantify how much time the mouse spends in different regions of the maze.

We assume you are already familiar with the [`movement` dataset structure](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/movement_dataset.html) and the [`movement` GUI](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/gui.html), both introduced in @sec-movement-intro.

::: {.callout-note title="Using the right environment"}

If you are following along this chapter on your own computer,
make sure to run all code snippets with the `animals-in-motion-env` environment activated
(see [prerequisites @sec-install-movement]). This also applies to launching the
`movement` graphical user interface (@sec-movement-gui).

:::

```{python}
#| include: false
import xarray as xr

xr.set_options(
    display_expand_attrs=False,
    display_expand_coords=False,
    keep_attrs=True,
)
```

## The elevated plus maze

The [EPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevated_plus_maze) is a simple maze in the shape of a plus sign, raised on a platform above the ground. It consists of four arms radiating from a central square: two opposite "open arms" (corridors without walls) and two opposite "closed arms" (corridors enclosed by walls). Mice are generally averse to open, exposed spaces, so they tend to prefer the closed arms.
The proportion of time spent in the open arms is therefore commonly used as a measure of anxiety-like behaviour: the more time spent in the open arms, the less anxious the mouse.

::: {.callout-note title="Acknowledgement"}
Thanks to Loukia Katsouri (Sainsbury Wellcome Centre) for sharing this dataset with us.
:::

## Load and inspect the data

First, let's import everything we need:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from movement import sample_data
from movement.filtering import filter_by_confidence, rolling_filter
from movement.plots import plot_occupancy
from movement.roi import compute_region_occupancy, load_rois
```

Next, let's load the data. In @sec-movement-intro we loaded pose tracks from a file on disk.
Here, we'll get the EPM data from one of `movement`'s [sample datasets](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/input_output.html#target-sample-data).

::: {.callout-note title="Sample datasets"}
These datasets are a curated collection of tracking outputs from various species and software, which are downloaded on demand and cached under `~/.movement/data`.
:::

We use
[`fetch_dataset()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.sample_data.fetch_dataset.html) and pass `with_video=True` so that the associated video is downloaded as well—we'll need it later.

```{python}
ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset(
    "DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5",
    with_video=True,
)
ds
```

These are [DeepLabCut](https://www.mackenziemathislab.org/deeplabcut) predictions for a single mouse, with 8 keypoints tracked over roughly 10 minutes at 30 fps.

Along with the pose tracks, this sample dataset comes with a video and a still frame extracted from it.
Their paths are stored as attributes of the dataset:

```{python}
print(ds.frame_path)
print(ds.video_path)
```

Take note of these paths—we'll need them to later draw regions of interest in the GUI.

Let's also have a look at the still frame, to get a sense of the maze we are dealing with:

```{python}
#| label: fig-epm-frame
#| fig-cap: "A still frame from the video, showing the elevated plus maze from above."

frame = plt.imread(ds.frame_path)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(frame)
ax.set_title("Elevated plus maze")
```

The camera looks down on the maze from above. The two closed arms run vertically, while the two open arms are the bare horizontal platforms extending left and right from the central square.

## Clean the data

Pose estimation output inevitably contains low-confidence or erroneous predictions, especially around occluded body parts.
This is the case for our dataset, so some cleaning is in order before we analyse the data.

We saw an example of how to clean the data in @sec-movement-intro. This time we can have a go at coding the data cleaning steps ourselves.

::: {.exercise-prompt}
Clean the pose tracks:

1. Discard predictions with a confidence score below `0.95`, using
   [`filter_by_confidence()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.filter_by_confidence.html).
   Which keypoint loses the most data? Does that make sense given the geometry of the maze?
2. Smooth the result with a rolling **median** filter, using
   [`rolling_filter()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.rolling_filter.html) and a window of length 5 frames. Set `min_periods=2`, so that a smoothed value is produced whenever at least 2 of the 5 frames in the window are present (rather than requiring all 5).

Call the cleaned position array `position_clean`—we'll use it for the rest of the chapter.
:::

::: {.exercise-solution}

```{python}
position_conf = filter_by_confidence(
    ds.position,
    ds.confidence,
    threshold=0.95,
    print_report=True,
)

position_clean = rolling_filter(
    position_conf,
    window=5,
    statistic="median",
    min_periods=2,
)
```

In terms of number of samples dropped, the `snout` keypoint seems the worst affected, followed by `tail_end`. This makes sense: the snout could often be occluded by the mouse's head if it pitches forward, and the tail end is a fine feature that may be hard to distinguish from the background.
:::

## Visualise space occupancy

Before defining any regions of interest, it's worth getting a global impression of where the mouse spent its time.

In @sec-movement-intro, we relied on `xarray`'s built-in plotting methods.
The [`movement.plots`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.plots.html) module adds a few convenient plotting functions on top of those, tailored to motion tracking data.
One of them is
[`plot_occupancy()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.plots.plot_occupancy.html),
which draws a 2D histogram of position. With default arguments, it computes the histogram of the centroid of all keypoints.

::: {.callout-note title="Multiple individuals"}
If the dataset contains more than one individual, the centroid data of all individuals is pooled before computing the histogram by default. To plot a subset instead, pass the `individuals` argument (and `keypoints`, to restrict which keypoints go into the centroid).
:::

We'll overlay the histogram on the still frame that came with the dataset, so we can see the maze geometry underneath.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-epm-occupancy
#| fig-cap: "Occupancy of the mouse's centroid across the maze, on a logarithmic colour scale."

frame = plt.imread(ds.frame_path)
height, width = frame.shape[:2]

# Bins of 30x30 pixels, covering the whole frame
bin_size = 30
bins = [
    np.arange(0, width + bin_size, bin_size),
    np.arange(0, height + bin_size, bin_size),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(frame)

plot_occupancy(
    position_clean,
    ax=ax,
    bins=bins,
    alpha=0.8,
    cmin=10,  # hide bins with fewer than 10 frames
    norm="log",
)

# Match the axes to the frame, keeping the image orientation
ax.set_xlim(0, width)
ax.set_ylim(height, 0)
ax.set_title("Occupancy heatmap")
ax.collections[0].colorbar.set_label("# frames")
```

Beyond `individuals`, `keypoints` and `ax`, any keyword arguments are passed on to
[`matplotlib`'s `hist2d`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.hist2d.html),
which is where `bins`, `cmin` and `norm` come from.
The logarithmic colour scale is worth the extra argument here: without it, the few heavily visited bins would flatten everything else to a single colour.

The trajectories reflect the underlying plus shape of the maze. The centre of the maze seems to be one of the most visited areas. But to inspect region occupancy in further detail, we need to define these regions explicitly.

## Define ROIs in napari {#sec-epm-napari}

A region of interest (ROI) is a shape defined in the same pixel coordinates as the tracking data. By combining ROIs with pose tracks, we can relate the animal's position to meaningful areas of the camera view, and answer questions such as whether the mouse was inside a given arm of the maze at a given time.

The easiest way to define a region of interest is using the `movement` GUI (see @sec-movement-gui if you need a refresher).

::: {.exercise-prompt}
Draw the regions of the maze in the GUI and save them to a file.

The steps below are a condensed version of the [define regions of interest](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/gui.html#define-regions-of-interest) section of the `movement` GUI guide, which happens to use this very dataset for its screenshots. You can refer to the guide for the more detailed steps.

1. Launch the GUI from the command line with `movement launch`.
2. Load a background layer: drag and drop either the video or the still frame onto the viewer, using the paths we printed above.
3. Expand the "Define regions of interest" menu on the right-hand side, and click "Add new layer". This adds a napari [shapes layer](https://napari.org/stable/howtos/layers/shapes.html) named "regions", managed by `movement`.
4. With that layer selected, press <kbd>P</kbd> to activate the polygon tool and draw around one region of the maze, clicking once per vertex. Each shape you draw appears as a row in the regions table.
5. Repeat until you have five regions: the two open arms (left and right), the two closed arms (top and bottom), and the central square.
6. Double click the name cell of each row to rename it. We'll use `open_arm_left`, `open_arm_right`, `closed_arm_top`, `closed_arm_bottom` and `centre`.
7. Click "Save layer" and save the regions to a `.geojson` file.

:::

::: {.exercise-solution}
You can compare your `geojson` file with the set of regions we prepared earlier: [EPM_rois.geojson](data/EPM_rois.geojson){download="EPM_rois.geojson"}. Since drawing regions is a manual task, there will be differences. To see how the boundaries compare, you can load both files into the GUI with "Load layer".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="`napari` shapes and `movement` regions"}
Any [`napari` shape](https://napari.org/stable/howtos/layers/shapes.html) can become a `movement` region, but the resulting object in `movement` depends on what you drew:
polygons, rectangles and ellipses become
[`PolygonOfInterest`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.PolygonOfInterest.html) objects,
while lines and paths become
[`LineOfInterest`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.LineOfInterest.html) objects.
The latter are useful for boundaries an animal may cross, rather than areas it may occupy.
:::

## Load and visualise ROIs

We can now read the regions we defined in the GUI into Python with
[`load_rois()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.load_rois.html).

For reproducibility, we'll use a set of regions we prepared earlier and stored in the book's repository. But feel free to have a go with your own ROIs, the results should not change dramatically.

```{python}
rois = load_rois("data/EPM_rois.geojson")

[roi.name for roi in rois]
```

The variable `rois` is a list of region objects, each carrying its **name** and sequence of **vertices**:

```{python}
print(rois[0])
```

Additionally, every region can draw itself onto a `matplotlib` axes with its
[`plot()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.PolygonOfInterest.html#movement.roi.PolygonOfInterest.plot)
method. This is very helpful to double check that our regions line up with the maze.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epm-rois
#| fig-cap: "The five regions of interest drawn over the EPM."

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(frame)

for roi, colour in zip(rois, plt.cm.Dark2.colors, strict=False):
    roi.plot(ax, facecolor=colour, alpha=0.5)

ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize="small")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Beyond plotting: geometric variables"}
A `PolygonOfInterest` also has methods to compute convenient geometric variables such as:

* the distance from a point to a region's boundary,
* the nearest point on a boundary, or
* the angle at which an animal approaches a region.

See the [`movement.roi`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.html) API reference and the [boundary angles example](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/examples/boundary_angles.html) for what's possible.
:::

## Compute time spent in each ROI

To inspect whether the mouse was in a region of space or not, we need to define what "being in a region" means. The simplest approach is to reduce the mouse to a single point. It's not the only option though: one could instead ask whether *any* keypoint falls inside a region, or what fraction of the keypoints do, for example. But reducing the mouse to a single point is simple enough, so we do that here.

As that point, we'll use the centroid of all keypoints, computed as we did in @sec-movement-intro.

```{python}
centroid = position_clean.mean(dim="keypoint")
```

We can now compute the occupancy in each of the ROIs we defined, by passing the centroid and the regions to
[`compute_region_occupancy()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.compute_region_occupancy.html).

```{python}
occupancy = compute_region_occupancy(centroid, rois)
occupancy
```

If you inspect the output closely, you will notice the output array mirrors the input `centroid` array, except that the `space` dimension has been replaced by a **`region` dimension**. Moreover, the coordinates of this region dimension are the **region names** we assigned in the GUI.
You will also notice the output `occupancy` is a boolean array: `True` where that point was inside that region at that time, `False` otherwise.

We can use the `occupancy` boolean array to directly compute the proportion of time spent in each region, by summing over time and dividing by the number of frames.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epm-time-per-region
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of the session the mouse's centroid spent in each region."

time_per_region = 100 * occupancy.sum("time") / occupancy.sizes["time"]
time_per_region = time_per_region.squeeze()  # drop the single-individual dim

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(time_per_region.region.values, time_per_region.values)
ax.set_ylabel("% time spent in region")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Why don't the percentages add up to 100%?"}
If you inspect the `time_per_region` variable, you may notice the percentages don't add up to 100%.

```{python}
print(f"Accounted for: {float(time_per_region.sum()):.1f}% of frames")
```

The denominator is the total number of frames, but not every frame is counted in some region. A frame contributes to no region at all if the centroid is `NaN` (position missing after cleaning), or if it falls in a part of the arena we didn't cover with a region.

:::

This mouse spent a comparable amount of time in the open and closed arms, and a sizeable fraction of the session in the centre.

::: {.exercise-prompt}
As discussed, the centroid is not the only way to represent the overall position of the mouse.

1. Recompute the occupancy using the `tailbase` keypoint alone instead of the centroid, and plot the two sets of percentages side by side. 
2. How do occupancy times change? Can you infer why?

:::

::: {.exercise-solution}

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Time spent in each region, using the centroid or the tailbase to represent the mouse."

tailbase_occupancy = compute_region_occupancy(
    position_clean.sel(keypoint="tailbase"), rois
)
time_per_region_tailbase = (
    100 * tailbase_occupancy.sum("time") / tailbase_occupancy.sizes["time"]
).squeeze()

x = np.arange(time_per_region.sizes["region"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(x - 0.2, time_per_region.values, width=0.4, label="centroid")
ax.bar(x + 0.2, time_per_region_tailbase.values, width=0.4, label="tailbase")
ax.set_xticks(x, time_per_region.region.values, rotation=30)
ax.set_ylabel("% time spent in region")
ax.legend()
```

The time spent in the centre region increases when using the `tailbase` keypoint rather than the centroid, whereas the time spent in the open arms decreases. The closed arms show less variation.

This makes sense: the tailbase trails behind the mouse, so it is still in the centre while the snout and the rest of the keypoints in the body have already entered an arm. And the effect is strongest for the open arms, which the mouse tends to enter only partway before turning back.

Note as well that the `tailbase` accounts for noticeably fewer frames:
```{python}
print(f"centroid: {float(time_per_region.sum()):.1f}%")
print(f"tailbase: {float(time_per_region_tailbase.sum()):.1f}%")
```

The centroid is the average of up to 8 keypoints and is only `NaN` when all of them are missing, whereas a single `tailbase` keypoint missing makes that frame unusable.
:::

## Counting entries and exits
The time spent in a region is an aggregate metric across the full trial. We may be interested in inspecting how this dwell time was accumulated throughout the trial instead. For that, the number of entries into each region is a useful complement, and it comes almost for free from the boolean array we already have.

If we compute the consecutive differences of the `occupancy` array along the time dimension, we get an array that for each frame holds a `1` if that frame was an "entry", a `-1` if that frame was an "exit", or `0` if it was neither.

```{python}
transitions = occupancy.astype(int).diff(dim="time")

entries = (transitions == 1).sum("time").squeeze()
exits = (transitions == -1).sum("time").squeeze()

for region in entries.region.values:
    print(
        f"{region:<20} "
        f"entries: {int(entries.sel(region=region)):>4} "
        f"exits: {int(exits.sel(region=region)):>4}"
    )
```

Entries and exits are nearly balanced for each region. This is a useful sanity check: within the session, every entry into a region must be followed by an exit, and every exit preceded by an entry. The only frames that can break the pairing are the first and the last: if the mouse is already inside a region at the start of the session, its first departure is an exit with no matching entry, and if it is inside a region at the end, its last arrival is an entry with no matching exit. So the two counts should match exactly, or differ by exactly one if the pairing is broken. A larger mismatch between the counts would suggest something went wrong in how we derived the transitions.

The centre is entered far more often than any arm, which is what you would expect from an animal that repeatedly ventures a short way into an arm and returns.

::: {.callout-note title="Spurious entries and exits"}
Be aware that this simple count has some spurious effects. 

Missing data is one source of these: the centroid is `NaN` wherever the position could not be recovered after cleaning, and `compute_region_occupancy()` marks those frames as `False`. A tracking gap while the mouse sits well inside a region therefore looks exactly like a brief exit followed by a re-entry. 

Tracking jitter around a boundary is another: a centroid that wobbles in and out across an edge adds an entry and an exit for every wobble.

Note that neither source breaks the balance we checked above, since both add entries and exits in pairs. To guard against them, we could discard visits shorter than some minimum duration, and handle gaps explicitly rather than letting them count as time spent outside.
:::
